client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother died last year — it was a car accident, and it just kind of... shattered everything. Things I used to enjoy, like going out with friends or even just watching a movie, feel completely hollow now. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: What you've been carrying since losing your brother — that profound sense of hollowness, the way things that once brought joy now feel empty — makes complete sense after such a sudden, devastating loss. I want you to know that reaching out, even with doubt that it will help, takes real courage, and I'm genuinely glad you're here. I'm curious, when you say things feel "hollow," is there a particular moment or activity recently where that feeling hit you the hardest?

client: It was last Sunday, actually. I used to watch football with my brother every weekend — it was kind of our thing — and I turned on the game without thinking, and then just... sat there staring at the screen feeling like I was in the wrong place at the wrong time. I turned it off after about ten minutes because it felt almost disrespectful to enjoy it without him.
therapist: That moment sounds incredibly painful — what was once a cherished connection with your brother suddenly became a reminder of his absence, and it makes so much sense that it felt unbearable to sit with. I want to gently explore that thought that enjoying it felt "disrespectful," because grief can sometimes convince us that moving forward or finding moments of joy means we're betraying the people we've lost — when in reality, those shared rituals can also be a way of honoring them. What do you think your brother would have wanted for you in that moment, if he could have been there?

client: I've thought about that before, actually — what he would have wanted. And honestly, I know he would have wanted me to enjoy it, to laugh, to keep watching those games like we always did. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling okay about it are two completely different things, and I don't know how to close that gap.
therapist: You've just named something really profound — that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is one of the most honest and difficult parts of grief, and it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong. The fact that you can already hear your brother's voice wanting good things for you is actually something meaningful to hold onto, even when it doesn't yet reach your heart. I wonder, what do you think gets in the way in those moments — is it more a feeling of guilt, or something closer to sadness that he isn't physically there to share it with you?

client: I think it's honestly both, but if I had to pick one that hits harder in the moment, it's the guilt. Like, there's this voice that says I don't deserve to feel good when he can't, that enjoying something is almost a betrayal of how much I miss him. The sadness is there too, but the guilt is the one that kind of shuts everything down before it even starts.
therapist: That voice telling you that you don't deserve to feel good is such a common but painful part of grief, and I want you to know it's not the truth about you — it's your love for your brother looking for somewhere to go. It's actually worth noticing that the guilt and the love feel tangled together right now, as if enjoying life and honoring how much you miss him feel like opposites, when they don't have to be. I'm wondering — when that guilty voice shows up, does it sound like *your* voice, or does it remind you of anything or anyone else?

client: That's... a really strange question, actually, because I hadn't thought about it that way before. When I sit with it, the voice kind of sounds like me, but also like this version of me that my brother would have argued with — he always used to call me out when I was being too hard on myself. I guess that makes it feel even more confusing, because it's like I'm doing the thing he hated, and he's not here to push back anymore.
therapist: That's such a tender and important insight — in a way, you've just described losing not only your brother, but also the person who helped balance out that harsh inner voice, which means the loss is even deeper than it might have first appeared. And there's something quietly powerful in what you've noticed: a part of you already *knows* he would push back on that guilt, which means his perspective isn't entirely gone — it lives in you, even if it's harder to access right now. I'm curious whether, in a moment when that guilty voice gets loud, you might be able to experiment with asking yourself what your brother would actually say back to it — do you think that feels possible, even just as a small try?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that could work, but honestly it feels almost painful to try to imagine his voice right now because it just reminds me how much I miss him. Like, I'm worried that instead of it helping, it'll just open up this huge wave of grief and I won't be able to function. I don't know if I'm ready to go there yet.
therapist: That's really important feedback, and I'm glad you told me — pushing toward something that doesn't feel safe yet isn't the right move, and your instinct to protect yourself deserves respect, not pressure. What you're describing, that fear of being overwhelmed by a wave of grief you won't be able to manage, is something we can work with gently and at your own pace, without forcing open any doors before you're ready. I'm wondering, are there smaller moments in your day where you feel even slightly more like yourself, where the grief loosens its grip just a little — even briefly?

client: I appreciate that you're not pushing me, that actually helps a little. But when you ask about moments where I feel more like myself... I honestly have to think hard, because most days just blur together in this gray kind of fog. There are maybe brief flashes, like when I'm making coffee in the morning before I fully wake up and remember everything, but then it hits me again and I feel almost guilty for having had that second of peace.
therapist: That moment with the coffee — that small, quiet second before the weight rushes back in — is actually really significant, because it tells us that some part of you is still capable of peace, even if it feels fleeting and even if the guilt quickly follows. And I notice that guilt seems to show up almost like a guard, swooping in whenever you get even a brief moment of relief, as if it's trying to make sure you never stray too far from the grief. I'm curious — what do you think that guard is trying to protect, or what does it fear might happen if you allowed yourself that second of peace without punishing yourself for it?

client: I've never really thought about it that way before — like the guilt is actually doing something, serving some kind of purpose. But when you put it like that, I think maybe... if I let myself feel okay, even for a second, it feels like I'm saying that losing my mom wasn't that big a deal, like I'm moving on too fast and leaving her behind. It's almost like the guilt is the last thread connecting me to her, and if I let it go, I'm terrified there'll be nothing left.
therapist: I want to gently reflect something back to you — you've been talking about your brother, but just now you said your mom, and I don't want to gloss over that in case there's something important there. Whatever the connection, what you've just described is one of the most profound fears in grief — that releasing the pain means releasing the person, as if the hurt is the last proof that they mattered. I want you to know that the love itself, the memories, the way they shaped who you are, those things don't disappear when the guilt loosens its grip — but I'm wondering, does it feel true to you that the guilt is the *only* thread still connecting you to them?

client: I noticed I said mom... I don't even know why that slipped out, maybe because the loneliness feels the same, like they're both just... gone in different ways. And no, I don't think the guilt is the only thread, but it's the loudest one, the one that keeps waking me up at 3am and making me feel like I'm still in it somehow. I guess I'm scared that if the guilt quiets down, I'll just be left with this empty silence, and that feels even worse than the pain.
therapist: That slip feels meaningful — grief has a way of collapsing our losses together, and it sounds like there may be more layers here than just your brother, which we can explore gently whenever you feel ready. What you just said about the empty silence feeling worse than the pain is one of the most honest things someone can say, because it names the real fear underneath the guilt — not that you'll stop hurting, but that you'll stop *feeling connected*. I want to sit with that for a moment and ask: are there any threads to him — or to her — that feel quieter than the guilt but maybe more gentle, like a memory or something they gave you that still feels warm rather than painful?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to go straight to the hard stuff, the last phone call, the things I didn't say. But there is this one thing — my brother used to send me these completely random texts, like a photo of a weird cloud or a joke that made no sense out of context, and for some reason I never deleted them. I don't open that thread very often because I'm scared of what I'll feel, but I guess just knowing it's there is... I don't know, it's something.
therapist: What you just described — those random texts, the weird clouds, the jokes that made no sense — that *is* a thread, and it sounds like a really tender and true one, because it captures something alive about who he was rather than the weight of the loss. The fact that you've kept them without even needing to open them tells me that some part of you already knows how to hold onto him in a way that isn't only pain. I'm wondering, what does it feel like just to acknowledge right now, in this moment, that those texts exist and that keeping them has been its own quiet act of love?
